replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: an AI doesn't read your words.

It never sees letters at all.

[KEY]LLMs convert text into numbers before doing anything else — a process called **tokenization**.[/KEY]

When you type a prompt, the model's first job is to chop your text into chunks called *tokens*. A token is roughly a word or word-piece — "running" might stay as one token, but "unbelievable" might split into two or three. Each token then gets swapped for a number from the model's vocabulary.

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. So every word or fragment you type maps to one of those ~100,000 slots — just a number in a list.[/EX]

That list of numbers is what actually travels into the model. No letters, no spaces, no punctuation as you know it — just a sequence of IDs.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually hand off to the rest of the model?
A) The original words you typed, preserved exactly
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A search query sent to the internet
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never touches raw text again after that handoff.

Now here's where it gets interesting. A list of numbers isn't enough on its own — the model also needs to know what those numbers *mean* and how they relate to each other.

That's where **attention** comes in.

The attention mechanism lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide which ones matter most for figuring out its meaning.

[EX]Take the word "bank." Same token whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution. But in "I sat on the bank of the river," attention pulls hard toward "river" — and that's what settles the meaning. In "I put cash in the bank," attention pulls toward "cash" instead. The word alone is ambiguous; the context resolves it.[/EX]

[KEY]**Attention** is the mechanism that connects each token to the other tokens that give it meaning.[/KEY]

After attention does its work across all the tokens, the model has a rich, context-aware picture of your whole prompt — and it's ready to do something with it.

[Q]
Why can't the model just look at each token one at a time, in order, without attention?
A) It would run too slowly on modern hardware
B) Individual tokens are often ambiguous — meaning only emerges from context
C) Tokens aren't numbers yet at that stage
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) Tokens aren't numbers yet at that stage
replies.raw:
Not quite — tokens are already numbers by this point. The tokenizer handles that conversion first, before attention ever runs. C describes the step *before* tokenization, which is already done.

The real issue is about **meaning**, not format.

Think back to "bank." The number for that token is the same whether you're near a river or a cash machine. A model reading tokens one by one, with no way to peek at neighbors, would have no way to sort that out.

It needs to see the whole context at once — that's exactly the job attention does.

[Q]
Why can't the model just look at each token one at a time, in order, without attention?
A) It would run too slowly on modern hardware
B) Individual tokens are often ambiguous — meaning only emerges from context
C) Tokens aren't numbers yet at that stage
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Individual tokens are often ambiguous — meaning only emerges from context
replies.raw:
You've got it — context is everything, and attention is how the model reads it.

Now for the final piece: what does the model actually *do* with all that context?

It makes a prediction — specifically, it predicts the single most likely **next token**.

After attention has built a rich picture of your prompt, the model outputs a probability score for every token in its vocabulary. The highest-scoring token gets picked, appended to the sequence, and then the whole process runs again — one token at a time, until the response is done.

[EX]Give a model the prompt "The cat sat on the ___" and it will assign very high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." The context makes some continuations overwhelmingly likely.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text by predicting the most probable **next token**, one at a time, using everything that came before.[/KEY]

One nuance worth knowing: as of 2026, Anthropic's interpretability research found that Claude can sometimes plan a few tokens ahead — for instance, picking a rhyming word before writing the line that leads up to it. So "purely one token at a time" is the basic picture, but it's a little more subtle than that.

[Q]
What is the model actually outputting each step of generation?
A) A complete sentence assembled all at once
B) A probability distribution over every possible next token
C) A search result retrieved from its training data
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
That's a sharp way to put it — and you're right. That's exactly the logic we'll use.

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise:

---

Consider this sentence, which an LLM is completing one token at a time:

**"She opened the dishwasher and pulled out a clean ___."**

1. Pick ONE slot in this sentence where the model would predict with **high confidence** — where one continuation dominates. Name the word or phrase that fills it, and explain why training data makes it dominant.

2. Pick ONE slot where the model would predict with **low confidence** — where several continuations are equally plausible. Name at least two words that could fit, and explain why no single one dominates.

3. The sentence ends mid-thought: *"She opened the dishwasher and pulled out a clean ___ and then suddenly ___."* What happens to the model's confidence at that second blank, and why?

replies.user: Naming the exact spots: high confidence — the final word of your sentence, because the phrase leading into it is a fixed expression. Low confidence — immediately after the first word, because almost any word class could follow there.
replies.raw:
Good instincts on the high-confidence slot — "clean ___" after a dishwasher context does narrow things down hard, and you're right that the phrase creates a strong pull toward specific completions like "plate" or "glass."

But I want to push back a little on the low-confidence pick.

"She" as a first word is actually followed by a pretty constrained set of options — verbs, mostly, and common ones at that ("opened," "walked," "said," "looked"). That's not a wide-open slot.

A genuinely low-confidence slot would be somewhere the *semantic* context leaves things open — like the blank at the end of your sentence. After "clean ___" in a dishwasher context, "plate," "glass," "fork," "cup," and "bowl" are all plausible and roughly equal. No single one dominates.

And you didn't address part 3 — what happens at that second blank ("and then suddenly ___") and why.

Give that one a go: does confidence go up or down there, and what's the reason?

replies.user: Right — and that's why it can be confidently wrong: plausible isn't the same as true. It optimizes for likely text, not verified facts.
replies.raw:
That's a genuinely important insight, and it'll matter a lot in later lessons — but it's your observation, not an answer to part 3 yet.

Back to the question: in the sentence **"She opened the dishwasher and pulled out a clean ___ and then suddenly ___,"** what happens to the model's confidence at that second blank ("and then suddenly ___"), and why?

Think about what "suddenly" signals to a model trained on enormous amounts of human writing — does it narrow things down, or open them up?

**"…and then suddenly ___."**

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: an AI doesn't read your words.

It never sees letters at all.

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens when you hit send. Your text gets sliced into chunks called *tokens* — not quite words, not quite letters, something in between.

[EX]"playing" might become two tokens: "play" + "ing". A space before a word often becomes part of the next token. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these chunks.[/EX]

[KEY]Every token gets converted to a number, because math is the only thing a neural network can actually do.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as its input when you type a prompt?
A) The letters of your message, one character at a time
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A recording of your voice converted to text
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never touches raw letters, only numbers.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't just sit in a list — they get placed in a kind of **meaning space**.

Words with similar meanings end up close together in this space. "King" and "queen" are neighbors. "Bank" (money) and "bank" (river) are the same token — but the model figures out which meaning applies by paying attention to the surrounding tokens.

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river," the token "river" pulls the meaning of "bank" toward water. In "I put cash in the bank," the token "cash" pulls it toward finance. The word "bank" alone, with no context, is genuinely ambiguous — the surrounding tokens are what resolve it.[/EX]

[KEY]The attention mechanism lets each token "look at" other tokens in the sentence to figure out what it means in context.[/KEY]

[Q]
In the sentence "I went to the bank," which word resolves what "bank" means?
A) "went" — it signals movement toward a place
B) "to" — it signals direction
C) No word resolves it — the sentence is genuinely ambiguous
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) "went" — it signals movement toward a place
replies.raw:
Close instinct, but "went" and "to" just tell you someone moved somewhere — they don't tell you whether that somewhere is a financial institution or a riverbank.

"I went to the bank" is genuinely ambiguous. A word like "river" or "cash" nearby would resolve it, but neither is here.

[KEY]Attention needs *content* words — like "river" or "cash" — to disambiguate meaning; movement words like "went" and "to" don't carry enough signal.[/KEY]

Now for the third piece — what the model actually *does* with all this.

After attention sorts out meaning, the model makes a prediction: **what token should come next?**

It assigns a probability to every token in its vocabulary and picks from the top candidates. Some slots are easy — one word dominates. Others are wide open.

[EX]"The cat sat on the ___" strongly predicts "mat," "floor," or "couch" — a short list of likely tokens. But "My favorite color is ___" could end with hundreds of plausible tokens, so no single one dominates.[/EX]

[Q]
What does next-token prediction optimize for?
A) Finding the most truthful continuation
B) Finding the most plausible-sounding continuation
C) Retrieving the answer from a database
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Finding the most plausible-sounding continuation
replies.raw:
You nailed it — and that distinction between *plausible* and *true* turns out to matter a lot. It's why AI can sound confident while being wrong. But that's a later lesson.

You now have the full picture: tokens → numbers → attention → next-token prediction.

Let's put this to work.

---

**Here's your exercise.**

Read this sentence:

*"After years of study, she finally picked up her **bow** and performed for the crowd."*

1. The word "bow" could mean several things (a violin bow, a hair bow, a bow as in bending forward, a bow as in archery). Which meaning does the model land on here, and which specific tokens in the sentence drive that attention signal?

2. Now look at these two slots in the same sentence — rate each one HIGH confidence or LOW confidence for next-token prediction, and explain why:

   - The blank after *"picked up her bow and"* → what word comes next?
   - The blank after *"she finally"* → what word comes next?

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.

Back to the question:

2. For each of these two slots, is it HIGH or LOW confidence — and why does *this* sentence make it so?

   - After *"she finally"* → what word comes next?

Take a shot at both parts with the actual words from the sentence — your general principle is the right tool, just point it at the specific tokens.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: an LLM never actually reads your words.

It reads **numbers** — and the journey from your sentence to those numbers is where everything begins.

When you type a prompt, the very first thing that happens is your text gets chopped into chunks called *tokens*. A token is roughly a word or word-piece — "running" might stay as one token, or split into "run" + "ning," depending on the system.

[KEY]Every word you type is converted into a number before the model ever "sees" it.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens — each one mapped to a unique ID number. So "cat" becomes something like token #123, "sat" becomes #456, and so on. (The exact IDs vary by tokenizer, so treat those as illustrative.)[/EX]

Here's the check before we go further:

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your words into?
A) A compressed audio file the model can process
B) Numbers that represent words or word-pieces
C) A ranked list of synonyms for each word
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Numbers that represent words or word-pieces
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never touches raw text, only those numeric IDs.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Numbers alone don't capture *meaning* — after all, token #123 and token #124 are just neighbors on a number line, but "cat" and "dog" are more related to each other than either is to "democracy."

So the model converts each token ID into a **embedding** — a long list of hundreds or thousands of decimal numbers that positions the word in a kind of meaning-space.

Words used in similar contexts end up geometrically *close* to each other in that space.

[KEY]An embedding turns a token into a point in meaning-space, so the model can reason about how words relate.[/KEY]

[EX]"King" and "queen" end up near each other. "Bank" (money) and "bank" (river) get the *same* starting embedding — but the next step, attention, will sort out which meaning applies based on surrounding words like "cash" or "river."[/EX]

Here's your check on this idea:

[Q]
Why does the word "bank" need more than just its embedding to be understood correctly?
A) Because its embedding is stored differently depending on the sentence
B) Because embeddings only work for short words
C) Because the same token gets the same starting embedding regardless of meaning
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Because its embedding is stored differently depending on the sentence
replies.raw:
Close instinct — you're sensing that context matters, which is right. But the embedding itself doesn't change based on the sentence; "bank" gets the *same* starting embedding every time it enters the model.

What actually does the context-sorting work is a separate mechanism called **attention** — and that's exactly where we're headed next.

Attention lets the model look at every other token in your prompt and ask: *which ones should influence how I interpret this token right now?*

In "I sat on the bank of the **river**," attention pulls "river" strongly toward "bank" — and the model leans toward the waterside meaning. Swap in "cash" and attention shifts the whole interpretation.

[KEY]Attention is what lets the same word mean different things in different sentences — it weighs every surrounding token's influence.[/KEY]

[EX]"I went to the bank" on its own is genuinely ambiguous — "went," "to," and "the" don't decide it. There's no nearby "river" or "cash" for attention to grab onto, so the model stays uncertain about which sense applies.[/EX]

[Q]
What does the attention mechanism do with the other tokens in your prompt?
A) It deletes tokens that aren't relevant to the current word
B) It weighs how much each surrounding token should influence the current token's meaning
C) It translates each token into the language most common in the training data
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) It weighs how much each surrounding token should influence the current token's meaning
replies.raw:
You nailed it — attention is essentially a dynamic weighting system, pulling in the context that matters and downplaying what doesn't.

Now we can put the whole pipeline together with the final step: what the model actually *produces*.

After tokenization → embeddings → attention, the model outputs a **probability distribution** over its entire vocabulary. It's asking: given everything I've seen so far, what token is most likely to come next?

It picks one, appends it, then runs the whole process again — one token at a time, until it decides to stop.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by predicting the single most probable next token, then repeating that process from scratch.[/KEY]

[EX]Give a model "The cat sat on the ___" and it will assign very high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." The next token almost picks itself.[/EX]

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise:

---

Consider this sentence, which an LLM is completing one blank at a time:

**"The surgeon scrubbed her hands before entering the ___."**

**"She opened the ancient map and traced the route to the ___."**

1. For each blank, predict whether the LLM would assign **high confidence** or **low confidence** to its top next token.
2.

For each one, explain *why* — using what you now know about next-token prediction.

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
That's a sharp, accurate description of the principle — but I want to make sure you can *apply* it to these two specific sentences, not just state it in the abstract.

Back to the exercise:

**"The surgeon scrubbed her hands before entering the ___."**

**"She opened the ancient map and traced the route to the ___."**

1. For each blank, is the model's confidence **high** or **low**?
2.

For each one, explain why — pointing to what's in *that specific sentence* that makes continuations dominant or open.

Have a go at both sentences in your own words.

replies.user: Naming the exact spots: high confidence — the final word of your sentence, because the phrase leading into it is a fixed expression. Low confidence — immediately after the first word, because almost any word class could follow there.
replies.raw:
I want to make sure we're on the same page about which blanks you're analyzing — the exercise has two specific sentences, each with one blank at the end.

Back to the exercise:

**"The surgeon scrubbed her hands before entering the ___."**

**"She opened the ancient map and traced the route to the ___."**

For each sentence's blank:

1. High confidence or low confidence?

Why — what is it about *that sentence's* context that makes one continuation dominate, or leaves many equally plausible?

Take them one at a time if that helps.

replies.user: Right — and that's why it can be confidently wrong: plausible isn't the same as true. It optimizes for likely text, not verified facts.

replies.user: My takeaway: prompt → tokens → embeddings → attention weighs context → the model predicts one token at a time. That's why it feels fluent but doesn't 'know' things the way a database does.
